research_question: Does robust contrastive responsibility require an irreducibly agent-relative mode of representation, or can a rigid third-personal representation of an agent's intention and act suffice?
paper_title: God and the View From Nowhere: De Se Knowledge and Divine Omniscience

challenged_premise.text: A third-personal proposition identifying God as actualising a world does not itself represent that actualisation under the first-personal aspect required for source attribution.

paper_direction: A paper here would argue that the argument from divine contrastive responsibility to irreducible de se content depends on a substantive agency condition, not on the merely third-personal grammar or referential precision of divine cognition. It would develop the distinction between source-identifying knowledge and practically self-ascriptive representation, anticipate the rigid-identifier case in which G's intention selects and produces W1, and show either that this case lacks the agency-relative aspect required for robust responsibility or that no such additional aspect is needed. To succeed, the paper would need to state and defend a responsibility-relevant criterion that distinguishes treating an intentional act as an object of knowledge from representing it as one's own doing.

assessment.summary: There is a real issue here, but as framed it reruns the essential-indexical debate without engaging it and dodges the obvious reply that forming G's intention already requires de se self-ascription; pick a side, engage Perry and Cappelen–Dever, and say what is distinctive about the divine case.

revision.research_question: Does robust contrastive responsibility for actualising one world rather than another require irreducibly de se content in divine cognition, or can a rigid, de re representation of an agent's controlling intention and its act suffice when the agent's identity is not in doubt?
revision.paper_direction: A paper here would argue that the inference from divine contrastive responsibility to irreducible de se content fails, because robust responsibility requires only that the agent's intention be the operative control state for the outcome, and that a rigid, de re representation of that intention satisfies this requirement. The paper would defend the Cappelen-Dever style horn: the functional role of G's intention in selecting and producing W1 is sufficient for source attribution, so no irreducible first-personal mode of presentation is needed. It would make two moves. First, it would concede the referee's strongest point, that forming an intention to actualise W1 involves practical self-ascription, and then distinguish two things that point runs together: practical self-ascription as a feature of the control state (G's intention is G's, and G knows that G is the being whose intention is operative), which is de re and identity-preserving, and de se content as an irreducible mode of presentation that the attribution needs in order to be correct. Second, it would argue that the divine case changes the dialectic in a specific way. In the messy-shopper cases the case for de se content rests on an epistemic gap about who one is, and that gap is absent here, since G has no ignorance of identity and there is only one possible controller. Holding identity knowledge fixed therefore isolates the agency condition itself. The paper would then argue that any remaining case for irreducible de se content must rest on that condition alone, and that the condition is satisfied by the rigid case without residue. The paper would not claim that c008's literal claim is informative. Its target is the 'required for source attribution' clause, which the paper would restate as a claim about what robust responsibility minimally requires.

assessment.summary: There is a paper-shaped idea here, but its central claim that the divine case lacks an identity gap assumes the point at issue, and it would not survive a referee who knows Lewis's two-gods case until it shows how third-personal intention can guide action without self-location.

research_question: Can a similarity-relative parthood relation adequately track the metaphysical constituency denied by the traditional doctrine of divine simplicity?

challenged_premise.text: Instantiation can be modelled as parthood because objects may be understood as mereological fusions of their properties.

paper_direction: A paper here would argue that the symmetric-parthood formulation of divine simplicity succeeds only if its similarity-relative parthood relation is shown to represent the constituent relation excluded by traditional simplicity. It would distinguish the formal reconstruction from ordinary material composition, assess the proposed restriction to divine attributes, and anticipate the reply that formal modelling need not reproduce a physical inventory. To establish the thesis, it would need independently motivated criteria for relevant similarity-parts and an account of why those criteria make the relation sufficiently constituency-tracking, non-trivial, and resistant to contingent relational-property cases.

assessment.summary: There is a real question about whether a formal similarity-parthood relation captures what classical simplicity denies, but the copper-wire argument begs the question against constituent ontology and must be replaced by engagement with the traditional notion of metaphysical composition before this becomes a paper.

revision.research_question: Can a similarity-relative parthood relation, with relevance criteria taken from the tradition's own criteria of metaphysical composition (subject and accident, potency and act), model the constituency that classical divine simplicity denies?
revision.paper_direction: A paper here would argue that the symmetric-parthood formulation of divine simplicity succeeds only if its similarity-relative parthood relation tracks the metaphysical constituency the tradition denies, and that this condition is met only under relevance criteria drawn from the tradition itself. It drops the physical-inventory framing and treats the wire case as a test of a material reading that the instantiation premise does not assert. The paper would first fix a standard of traditional constituency, namely subject and accident and the composition of potency and act, and then state explicit relevance conditions for similarity-parts. It would then test whether those conditions exclude trivial mutual parthood between God and a divine attribute, and whether they exclude contingent relational properties, which are instantiated without composing the subject. If the relation fails either test, the paper would locate the failure precisely and state which restricted version of the symmetric formulation survives. The thesis is conditional and adequacy-based: it claims that the formulation is viable only under stated criteria, and it does not claim that the similarity-relative relation is already a faithful model of constituency.

assessment.summary: A reasonable adequacy question, but as proposed it defers its only real contribution and has not noticed that its traditional criteria presuppose a substance ontology that the property-fusion premise rejects; revise before writing.

research_question: Does robust contrastive responsibility require irreducibly de se representation of the selected outcome, or only representation of that outcome as resulting from an act the agent performs or selects?
paper_title: God and the View From Nowhere: De Se Knowledge and Divine Omniscience

challenged_premise.text: If an agent is robustly responsible for bringing about one outcome rather than another, its cognition must represent the first outcome as its own action.

paper_direction: A paper here would argue that the objection identifies a genuine equivocation between responsibility for an outcome and representing that outcome as an action: robust contrastive responsibility requires an agent-relative representation of the act–outcome relation, not self-representation of the distal outcome as an action. The case would develop the reservoir example and analogous ordinary agency cases, then anticipate the strongest reply that source attribution still requires a first-personal stance toward the selected act. It would need to show either that this stance is available in non-de-se terms, weakening the route to the divine conclusion, or that a principled feature of divine actualisation makes irreducible de se content necessary despite the revised premise.

assessment.summary: A clean counterexample to a carelessly worded premise, but it is easily repaired and does not reach the de se issue, so it would be dismissed as verbal unless rebuilt around whether source attribution can be non-de-se.

revision.research_question: Does robust contrastive responsibility require irreducibly de se representation of the selected outcome, or is agent-relative source attribution, represented in non-de-se terms, enough; and does divine basic action change that answer?
revision.paper_direction: A paper here would argue that the premise as literally stated, that the outcome must be represented as the agent's own action, is false, as the reservoir case shows. It would then argue that the repaired condition, that cognition represent the outcome as resulting from the agent's own act, is agent-relative but can in ordinary agency be met by non-de-se content: the agent describes the act-outcome link in general terms and identifies her own act de re through a perceptually given candidate, the spillway wheel she turns. The paper would then argue that the divine case removes that anchor, since actualising a world is not given among candidate acts and has no proximal/distal gap. It would test the two remaining routes. On the first, God knows de re that God actualises W1, which is non-de-se if God's self-identification is secured without a further self-locating fact. On the second, source attribution requires a first-personal identification of the act as one's own when no other anchor is available, which would make de se content irreducible. The paper would defend a conditional verdict: the divine conclusion holds only if basic actualisation is selected among alternatives and no non-indexical means of identifying it as God's own act is available. It would engage the Perry, Lewis and Castañeda literature on essential indexicals and the Kretzmann and Grim debates on omniscience and indexicals to decide whether that condition is met.

assessment.summary: The headline counterexample is a wording point that the argument's other premises already fix, and the real project is a reworking of the old omniscience-and-indexicals debate that still needs a coherent account of non-de-se self-identification before it is a paper.

research_question: Can instantiation be modelled as similarity-based parthood in a way that preserves the persistence of ordinary objects and supports the divine-simplicity application?

challenged_premise.text: Instantiation can be modelled as parthood because objects may be understood as mereological fusions of their properties.

paper_direction: A paper here would argue that the unrestricted fusion account of instantiation cannot support the divine-simplicity argument, because temporal change and shared properties expose missing identity and overlap conditions, while a restricted account may remain available for God's timeless essential properties. It would develop the lamp case to show why the original premise needs revision, anticipate Defender B's time-indexed-instance reply and Defender A's divine restriction, and determine whether either revision still supplies a coherent parthood relation capable of grounding the symmetry formulation. The paper would need to show either that the revised model has independently defensible persistence and identity conditions, or that its repairs make it too different or too weak to support the original argument.

assessment.summary: As framed, this restates textbook objections to bundle theory against a premise the argument only needs for a timeless God; it would need refocusing on the divine case, for example on circularity or on whether similarity-parthood really models instantiation, before it is a paper.

revision.research_question: Can similarity-based parthood, which permits mutual parthood, capture the instantiation relation between God and God's attributes, or does it yield only co-characterization? And does the symmetry formulation of divine simplicity survive once the parthood model is restricted to God's timeless essential properties?
revision.paper_direction: A paper here would argue that the parthood model of instantiation fails in the one domain where the divine-simplicity argument needs it, so the symmetry formulation can be stated but not grounded as a claim about instantiation. The paper drops the lamp-change case. Its target is the timeless divine case. It takes the premise under discussion in its restricted form: for God's essential properties, instantiation may be modelled as parthood. It then tests whether similarity-based parthood, as defined so that proper parthood is irreflexive, asymmetric and transitive for ordinary objects, and as permitting mutual parthood between God and omniscience while they remain numerically distinct, still expresses instantiation. Instantiation is directed: God is the bearer of omniscience, and not conversely. Mutual parthood makes the relation symmetric on the pair. The paper argues that the model therefore delivers co-characterization, a symmetric relation of shared characterization, unless it adds a direction-marking condition. Any such condition is a new primitive, and the paper shows that adding it either reintroduces the asymmetry that the symmetry formulation was meant to deny or leaves the relation without a principled ground. The paper also tests a second horn: whether defining proper parthood through similarity presupposes the simplicity thesis, because treating God's attributes as parts is only a substantive claim if the similarity relation is specified independently of the claim that God has no proper parts. The paper engages Paul's mereological bundle theory as the strongest version of the unrestricted view. It grants that Paul's acceptance of overlap through shared universals and the standard replies to change are coherent for ordinary objects. Its claim is that these replies do not transfer to God, since in the divine case the problem is directionality and not persistence. The paper concludes that the symmetry formulation is coherent as a formal thesis, but that the argument for it from instantiation-as-parthood is unsound unless the directionality problem is solved independently of the simplicity thesis.

assessment.summary: A workable topic with a clear structure, but its central dilemma ignores the defender's natural reply that collapsing the direction of predication is exactly what divine simplicity claims, and it must engage the Plantinga literature before it can stand.

research_question: Does robust contrastive responsibility require an agent to represent the selected outcome as attributable to that agent’s own exercise of control, and if so, must this representation contain irreducible de se content?
paper_title: God and the View From Nowhere: De Se Knowledge and Divine Omniscience

challenged_premise.text: Robust contrastive responsibility requires cognition that represents an outcome as issuing from the agent's own activity rather than relevant alternatives.

paper_direction: A paper here would argue that the move from robust contrastive responsibility to irreducible de se divine cognition depends on a stronger and presently unestablished source-attribution requirement. It would use cases such as Mira’s to distinguish impersonal representation of causal consequences, self-representation of an intended act, and representation of an outcome as attributable to one’s control; it would then assess whether only the last is necessary for responsibility. The strongest reply to anticipate is that practical deliberation already integrates agent, option, and outcome in a way that grounds attribution without explicit self-ascription. The paper would need to show either that this integration necessarily has irreducible de se content, or that responsibility can be grounded by act-level self-representation without the outcome-level de se representation required by the original argument.

assessment.summary: A tidy distinction built on a case whose own stipulated intention concedes the point, and whose best outcome still leaves the de se conclusion standing; not yet a publishable paper.

revision.research_question: Does robust contrastive responsibility require the agent's cognition to contain a representation of the selected outcome, or of the agent's act, as the agent's own, and if an act-level self-representation is what is required, is that content irreducibly de se, so that the inference to irreducible de se divine cognition holds?
revision.paper_direction: A paper here would argue that the inference from robust contrastive responsibility to irreducible de se divine cognition goes through only if the source-attribution requirement is located at the level of the agent's intended act and that act-level content is irreducibly first-personal. The Mira case cannot show that outcome-level self-representation is unnecessary, because the intention she is stipulated to have already represents the village outcome as to be brought about by her pulling A. The paper therefore drops the claim that the case refutes c006 and instead proves a conditional. It distinguishes three kinds of content: impersonal representation of causal consequences (A opens gate 1; gate 1 sends water to the quarry), act-level self-representation carried by an intention to pull A, and outcome-level representation of the outcome as issuing from one's control. It then argues that robust responsibility requires the second kind whenever the selection is deliberate, and that the impersonal display contributes only the contrastive knowledge. If the act-level content is reducible to impersonal content, c052 fails, since the required self-involvement can be fully specified without de se content. If it is irreducible, c052 survives and the paper shows that the divine case turns on whether God's act of actualising, which is identical to the outcome, admits act-level de se content. The irreducibility question is therefore the paper's central target, and it is addressed directly against the accounts of de se content in the literature (Perry, Lewis, Cappelen–Dever), not assumed.

assessment.summary: A tidy reframing that concedes the counterexample and then defers everything important to the existing de se debate; as it stands it is a literature-review-shaped conditional, not yet a publishable paper.

research_question: Does the inference from God's having no proper parts to God's being part of all of God's parts require bivalence or determinacy for the relevant parthood relation?

challenged_premise.text: If proper parthood is non-symmetric parthood, the claim that God has no proper parts yields the symmetry formulation of divine simplicity.

paper_direction: A paper here would argue that the symmetry formulation of divine simplicity is not entailed by the absence of proper parts unless the underlying parthood relation is bivalent or otherwise determinate. Its central case would be the three-valued countermodel, in which omniscience is part of God while the reverse relation is undetermined, so omniscience is not a proper part but reciprocal parthood does not follow. The strongest reply to anticipate is that the intended similarity-relative parthood relation already carries determinate structural features and that bivalence is only a clarification. The paper would need to show either that those features do not entail determinacy, making the repair substantively additional, or that an independently motivated semantics supplies determinacy and thereby restores the inference.

assessment.summary: As framed, this is a logic-textbook observation dressed up as an objection to divine simplicity; it becomes a paper only if the author can show that similarity-relative parthood is independently liable to indeterminacy.

revision.research_question: Does the inference from God having no proper parts to God being part of all of God's parts require bivalence or determinacy for the similarity-relative parthood relation, and under which definitions of 'proper part' does that dependence arise?
revision.paper_direction: A paper here would argue that the step from 'God has no proper parts' to the symmetry formulation of divine simplicity (God is part of all God's parts) holds under classical semantics, and fails only if the parthood relation admits truth-value gaps together with one specific definition of proper part, namely 'reverse parthood is false' rather than 'reverse parthood is not true'. The paper would proceed in three steps. First, it would show that under the 'not true' definition, and under strong Kleene evaluation, the three-valued countermodel does not falsify the conditional, because the antecedent is then false or undetermined, so the counterexample depends on a single definitional choice. Second, it would give an independent motivation for gaps: similarity comes in degrees, and similarity-relative parthood inherits that gradation, so some pairs such as 'God is part of omniscience' may lack a determinate value. This is a substantive claim the paper must argue, not assume. Third, it would state the result as a conditional: the symmetry formulation follows from the absence of proper parts whenever reverse parthood is bivalent for the relevant pairs. The central thesis is therefore a bounded claim about the dependence of the inference on bivalence, not a refutation of divine simplicity or of the classical argument.

assessment.summary: A clearly organised but thin proposal: its core result is a standard fact about three-valued logic, and it becomes a paper only if the author can show the target account is genuinely committed to indeterminate divine parthood.

research_question: Can an argument from the apparent randomness of history establish that visible moral patterns are not systematically dominant, and what standard would justify that aggregate judgment?
paper_title: DOES GOD EXIST? CAN WE TELL IF WE BASED THIS QUESTION ONLY UPON THE APPARENT RANDOMNESS OF EVERYTHING?

challenged_premise.text: Many apparently random historical events have identifiable biological, political, or social causes, yet their outcomes often appear morally indiscriminate and non-monotonic.

paper_direction: A paper here would argue that the argument from worldly randomness requires an explicit and independently supported aggregate premise about the distribution of morally intelligible outcomes in history. It would show that individual cases of harm structured by culpability, privilege, and power neither establish providence nor simply count as morally indiscriminate, while defending the claim that no reliable benevolent directional signature follows from their recurrence. The strongest reply to anticipate is that the relevant conclusion needs only inconsistency, not universal indiscriminacy; the paper would need to specify a standard for identifying moral patterns, justify the move from cases to an aggregate assessment, and explain why the resulting evidential profile underdetermines the rival worldviews.

assessment.summary: The counterexample does not touch a generic claim, and the proposed aggregate-premise demand ends up supporting the argument's modest underdetermination conclusion; as stated, this is not a paper.

revision.research_question: Does the apparent randomness of history, together with the absence of a directional moral signature, show that worldly evidence alone cannot decide between theism and naturalism? And can morally legible patterns produced by human culpability and power be separated from patterns that would bear on providence?
revision.paper_direction: A paper here would argue that the argument from worldly randomness does not need, and should not rest on, a generic aggregate claim about how often outcomes are morally indiscriminate. Its load-bearing premises are symmetry and absence: naturalism and biblical theology each explain apparent randomness through their own resources (impersonal causation and probability on one side; agency, natural processes, hidden providence, and delayed judgment on the other), and historical evidence lacks the directional signature a benevolently steered history would be expected to show. From these, the paper concludes that worldly evidence alone yields no clear winner, and that this conclusion is supported by evidential uncertainty rather than threatened by it. The paper would then state a principled criterion separating morally legible patterns produced by human agency from patterns relevant to providence. A pattern counts as human-agency-produced when it is fully accounted for by the culpability, privilege, and power of agents in the causal chain. A pattern counts as providence-relevant only if it displays desert-sensitive distribution that is not exhausted by those agents' choices. The bridge case illustrates the first category: the inspector's concealment and the mayor's policy fully account for who died and who was spared, so it is accommodated by both worldviews and does not discriminate between them. The paper would clarify 'non-monotonic' as outcomes whose harm does not vary in step with desert or culpability (for example, the more culpable are not uniformly the more harmed). It would argue that c001 survives only in this narrowed form, that the comparative assessment of theism and naturalism is settled by the combination of c002, c011, c038 and c039 rather than by any frequency claim, and that the bridge case shows the distinction does work but does not establish the frequency premise. The paper would not claim that theism predicts earthly moral tracking, and it would present the modest underdetermination conclusion as its actual result.

assessment.summary: This is a tidy repair of a weak premise, but it relocates rather than removes the unsupported aggregate claim and treats mutual accommodation as evidential parity, so the first competent reader would send it back.

research_question: Under what conditions can temporally bounded nonresistant nonbelief generate a non-duplicative package of goods whose net value exceeds the intrinsic value of the lost relationship with God?
paper_title: Divine Hiddenness, Greater Goods, and Accommodation

challenged_premise.text: Goods individually less valuable than a relationship with God can collectively make a world containing nonresistant nonbelief more valuable.

paper_direction: A paper here would argue that the many-goods response requires a net-of-overlap formulation and cannot rely on an unqualified aggregation of individually lesser goods. It would develop the case for comparing whole feasible histories, rather than merely counting named outcomes, while anticipating the strongest reply that shared dispositions and the intrinsic value of divine relationship make the goods non-additive or non-compensatory. To succeed, the paper would need to specify a defensible measure of non-duplicative value, defend the relevant counterfactual comparison with the God-relationship alternative, and identify a plausible bounded case in which the surviving package outweighs the lost relationship.

assessment.summary: The objection mostly shows that one example double-counts, which a defender can easily absorb; the paper is worth writing only if it moves to the real commensurability and counterfactual questions and does substantive work on them.

revision.research_question: Can a bounded period of nonresistant nonbelief generate a set of goods that is distinctive to nonbelief, where no feasible history within the relationship with God realizes those goods, and whose combined value, net of shared dispositional sources, exceeds the intrinsic value of the lost relationship?
revision.paper_direction: A paper here would argue for a bounded existential claim: there are feasible cases in which temporally limited nonresistant nonbelief yields several goods that are individually below the value of a relationship with God, that do not depend on one another's dispositional sources, and that together outweigh that relationship. The paper would not claim that most or typical cases succeed, and it would not defend the net-of-overlap formulation as a distinct thesis, since the referee is right that competent aggregation already assesses value net of overlap. Overlap instead becomes a constraint on case construction: a candidate case must show that its goods have separate sources. The paper would give three components. First, an axiological argument on commensurability: it would argue, against lexical priority of the relational good, that finite goods can in principle be compared with and outweigh a supreme relational good, and it would engage the existing axiological and greater-goods literature directly on this point. Second, a principled counterfactual test for distinctiveness: a good G counts as unavailable within the relationship only if every feasible history in which the agent is in that relationship and realizes G's core features requires an element the relationship cannot supply, such as the specific reconciliation that presupposes the prior estrangement. The claim that a relationship would cultivate the same disposition 'more deeply and more reliably' would be treated as a premise to be tested under this test, not assumed. Third, a worked bounded case with separate sources for each good, checked against the test, that shows the package outweighs the lost relationship under a stated value measure.

assessment.summary: A writable and respectable refinement of the many-goods reply, but it will stand or fall on whether the distinctiveness test can avoid trivial fine-grained individuation and whether the value comparison is set up as bounded delay rather than total loss.

research_question: Can a many-goods response to divine hiddenness count several goods arising from one person’s nonresistant nonbelief without treating their joint realization as an increase in nonbelief-related evil?
paper_title: Divine Hiddenness, Greater Goods, and Accommodation

challenged_premise.text: Multiple goods may arise from a single instance of nonresistant nonbelief without increasing that evil.

paper_direction: A paper here would argue that the many-goods response requires a comparative, episode-sensitive account of nonresistant nonbelief: several goods may support a single period of hiddenness only when their joint realization requires no additional nonbelief-related evil relative to available alternatives that secure an adequately comparable set of goods. The case would distinguish genuinely overlapping goods from goods distributed across a life and show why merely redescribing an extended deprivation as one instance does not settle its cost. It would anticipate the strongest reply that all goods can be consequences of one fixed interval, and would need to show either that the interval is necessary for the combined goods or that relevant alternatives impose equal or greater evil.

assessment.summary: A tidy but thin direction: as framed it misreads a modal premise and lands on a version of the standard necessity condition, so it needs a sharper target in the actual many-goods literature before it is a paper.

revision.research_question: Can a many-goods response to divine hiddenness count several goods arising from one person's nonresistant nonbelief without treating their joint realization as an increase in nonbelief-related evil, when the measure of that evil does not presuppose a sensus divinitatis account?
revision.paper_direction: A paper here would argue that the many-goods response can count several goods from one person's nonresistant nonbelief without increasing nonbelief-related evil only for goods whose required episodes are nested within a single continuous interval, and that goods requiring separated or non-nested episodes must be booked as additional evil. The argument has three parts. First, it shows that defenders of the many-goods response rely on a non-comparative count, in which everything that happens during one long deprivation is booked against one fixed evil, so that the cost of the deprivation is fixed by the life-span and not by what the goods require. Second, it sets out an episode-individuation criterion: an episode is a maximal continuous interval of nonresistant nonbelief, and a good is nested in an episode when its requirements fall wholly inside that interval. The measure of evil is the total extent of the minimal union of intervals that the joint bundle requires, weighted by a neutral depth index, such as the strength of unresisted absence of conviction, that does not presuppose any account of proper basicality. On this measure nested goods add no further episode, so their joint cost equals the cost of the longest-spanning requirement, which is already a cost on the ledger. Distributed goods that need separate episodes, or that need an interval longer than any single requirement, add measured evil. Third, the paper applies this to Maria's case. Her three goods are nested only to the extent that the search, the shared uncertainty, and the ethical crisis lie in one continuous interval. Where the crisis requires a stretch separated from the search by a period of resisting nonbelief, or where the solidarity good requires recurrence, the paper shows that the good's cost is an added episode rather than a re-description of one. The paper concedes that the modal premise survives only in its restricted, episode-sensitive form, and it anticipates the fixed-interval reply by showing that the interval is necessary for the combined goods only when the goods are nested. Where that condition fails, relevant alternatives that secure comparable goods must be shown to impose equal or greater evil.

assessment.summary: A tidy accounting proposal that, by its own lights, vindicates the modal premise it set out to challenge; it needs to show that the goods doing the real outweighing are non-nested before it becomes an objection rather than a footnote.

research_question: Can a many-goods response to divine hiddenness establish that the goods arising during a bounded episode of nonresistant nonbelief outweigh the relationship-loss of that episode once goods that require additional duration or severity are counted as part of its cost?
paper_title: Divine Hiddenness, Greater Goods, and Accommodation

challenged_premise.text: Multiple goods may arise from a single instance of nonresistant nonbelief without increasing that evil.

paper_direction: A paper here would argue that a viable many-goods response must distinguish goods that warrant the duration and severity of an episode of nonresistant nonbelief from goods that are genuinely co-realized at no additional relationship-loss. The case would show why aggregating all goods associated with an episode overstates the response when some goods require the episode to become longer or more anguished. It would anticipate the strongest reply: that bounded episodes can contain several cost-free goods and that temporary loss may still be outweighed. It would need to show either that such independently bounded episodes can be specified and valued in a way that supports the defense, or that the dependence of an episode’s cost on its goods makes the required aggregate comparison unavailable.

assessment.summary: A legitimate bookkeeping observation that misreads the modal strength of the challenged premise and does not yet answer the obvious net-value reply. It is not a paper until it argues that the bounding of episodes makes the aggregate comparison genuinely unavailable.

revision.research_question: Can the aggregate comparison that a many-goods response needs, between the goods of a nonresistant nonbelief episode and its relationship-loss, be made determinate when some of those goods require the episode to be longer or more severe, so that the episode's cost is not fixed independently of the goods it is said to justify?
revision.paper_direction: A paper here would argue that the modal claim that multiple goods may arise from a single episode of nonresistant nonbelief without increasing its evil survives the referee's objection, but that this modal claim does not by itself secure the aggregate comparison the many-goods response needs. The paper would grant that Mara's case shows only that some goods raise the cost, which is compatible with one cost-free co-realization. It would then argue that the net comparison, in which marginal goods are weighed against marginal evil, presupposes that an episode's duration and severity can be fixed independently of the goods it is said to contain. For goods whose realization depends on the episode's extent, such as the brother's slow choice, that presupposition fails. The episode's length is set by the goods it must realize, so the cost assigned to any given good depends on which goods are counted as belonging to the episode. Different selections of goods yield different baselines and different net values, so the aggregate comparison required by the collective-outweighing premise is indeterminate, or question-begging if the goods are used to fix the cost they are weighed against. The paper would develop this as a principled argument about individuation, not a reminder not to double-count, and would engage the greater-goods hiddenness literature on how goods are weighed against relationship-loss. It would conclude that the many-goods response can succeed only for episodes whose duration is specified independently of the goods they support, and that the response's collective claim is therefore restricted to such episodes.

assessment.summary: A clearly framed but misdiagnosed project: the interdependence of goods and episode cost undermines per-good cost attribution, not the aggregate comparison, so the indeterminacy thesis needs rebuilding before this is a defensible paper.

research_question: Can an analogy from vulnerable human love support a context-sensitive divine obligation to make relationship accessible to nonresistant persons without first establishing a general obligation of vulnerable love?
paper_title: Some critical reflections on the hiddenness argument

challenged_premise.text: Schellenberg's analogical route for P1 is successful only if he independently shows that a vulnerable God is obligated to make the beloved's access to relationship available, rather than merely permitted to do so.

paper_direction: A paper here would argue that the analogical route need not rest on a general obligation of vulnerable love, because context-sensitive obligations can be established through the features of particular loving relationships. It would develop the Mira case as a model of why expressed willingness, inability to initiate, and safe available contact can make withholding access a failure of care; it would then anticipate the strongest reply that these grounds may not transfer to God, especially if God can ensure eventual encounter without compromising dignity or safety. The paper would need to specify the relevant transfer conditions, explain their application to nonresistant nonbelief, and show whether permanent nonresistant nonbelief is compatible with perfect vulnerable love.

assessment.summary: As written, this objection misreads the premise and ends up conceding it; there might be a modest paper on transfer conditions for parental-love analogies, but it would have to be reframed and positioned against substantial existing literature.

revision.research_question: Can a grounds-based account of when withholding access from a beloved is a failure of care, drawn from particular vulnerable loving relationships, establish a context-sensitive duty for a perfectly loving God to make relationship accessible to nonresistant persons, and does that duty hold for every such person?
revision.paper_direction: A paper here would argue that vulnerable human love generates a duty to make relationship accessible when specified local grounds obtain: the beloved has expressed willingness to relate, cannot initiate contact for reasons other than their own resistance, and the lover can provide safe and available access. It would defend this grounds-based principle as an explicit bridge principle that is itself the context-sensitive obligation the analogical route requires, rather than a permission inferred from the Mira case, and it would argue that the Mira case illustrates the principle without establishing it on its own. The paper would then argue that these grounds can hold in the divine case for each nonresistant person, because they concern present access to relationship, which a reply appealing to eventual encounter does not supply, and because a perfectly knowing lover can assess each person's situation without a further general proof covering all circumstances. The paper would state its conclusion in narrowed form: the analogical route establishes a duty for every nonresistant person in whom the grounds obtain. Whether the grounds obtain universally, and whether permanent nonresistant nonbelief is compatible with perfect vulnerable love, are the points on which the universal form of P1 stands or falls, and the paper would identify them as such rather than assume them.

assessment.summary: A clearly organised but ultimately modest proposal: it turns the objection into a grounds-based bridge principle, then sets aside the transfer-to-every-person question on which any defence of P1's analogical route depends, so a competent referee would call it incomplete as it stands.

research_question: Can Schellenberg’s analogy for P1 preserve a Vanstonean conception of vulnerable divine love while establishing that God is obligated, absent overriding reasons, to make voluntary relationship genuinely accessible?
paper_title: Some critical reflections on the hiddenness argument

challenged_premise.text: Schellenberg’s analogical argument for P1 is unsuccessful because it distorts Vanstone’s vulnerable conception of divine love.

paper_direction: A paper here would argue that the Elena analogy undermines the claim that Schellenberg’s analogical route distorts vulnerable love, because costly self-disclosure that leaves acceptance free can itself be a form of kenotic vulnerability. The case would then distinguish that limited result from the stronger claim that perfect love obligates God to make relationship genuinely accessible. The strongest reply to anticipate is that the analogy establishes only permissible availability and leaves divine overriding reasons unresolved. The paper would need to show either that vulnerable perfect love generates a defeasible obligation of accessibility, together with principled limits on overriding reasons, or that Schellenberg’s argument can proceed on a weaker, non-exceptionless analogue of P1.

assessment.summary: A coherent but narrow point built on a disanalogous case: it needs a nonresistant-nonbeliever version of the example and a committed argument for obligation before it is a paper rather than a seminar response.

revision.research_question: Can Schellenberg's analogical route for P1 preserve a Vanstonean conception of vulnerable divine love when the analogue is a nonresistant beloved who lacks belief that the lover exists, and if so, does this support only a defeasible obligation of accessibility rather than the exceptionless P1?
revision.paper_direction: A paper here would argue that the Elena case, as originally framed, cannot show that Schellenberg's analogical route leaves vulnerable love intact, because Tomas is resistant and already believes Elena exists, so the case tests availability under resistance and not P1's claim about nonresistant nonbelief. The paper rebuilds the analogy around a nonresistant son who has never learned that his mother exists, or knows of her only uncertainly. It then asks whether the mother remains vulnerable if she secures belief-level accessibility, for example by making herself reliably and unmistakably known through a standing channel. The paper distinguishes two exposures: non-reception, the risk that a disclosure goes unregistered through no fault of the beloved, and non-response, the risk that a registered disclosure is refused. It argues that Vanstone's conception locates love's vulnerability chiefly in non-response, since the self-giving seeks a free answer, so guaranteeing reception does not by itself remove the exposure that makes love vulnerable. The paper must defend this claim against the rival view that non-reception is the core risk. It then gives a non-analogical bridge from vulnerable love to a defeasible obligation of accessibility: a lover whose aim is a free response has reason to secure the awareness that response presupposes, and this reason is overridable only by considerations that themselves respect the beloved's freedom. The paper engages Schellenberg's parent analogies and the existing literature on divine openness. It does not defend the exceptionless P1. The surviving thesis is that the analogy supports a defeasible obligation of accessibility that is compatible with vulnerable love.

assessment.summary: A coherent, writable refinement that answers the distortion charge in principle, but it stands or falls on an undefended reading of Vanstone and concedes enough on P1 that its payoff is modest.

research_question: Can a Molinist account of providence generate any observable historical signature of benevolent governance, or does it make the apparent distribution of suffering evidentially neutral?
paper_title: DOES GOD EXIST? CAN WE TELL IF WE BASED THIS QUESTION ONLY UPON THE APPARENT RANDOMNESS OF EVERYTHING?

challenged_premise.text: Historical evidence alone lacks the directional signature expected if history were steered toward the good.

paper_direction: A paper here would argue that Molinist providence undermines the claim that benevolent historical steering should produce a visible aggregate moral signature, while leaving open whether the resulting neutrality is principled or merely immunizing. The case would distinguish the failure of desert-tracking outcomes from the absence of all possible providential evidence, anticipate the reply that hidden providence and impersonal causation are simply evidentially ambiguous, and show either that Molinism supplies a non-arbitrary constraint on acceptable historical distributions or that c011 should be removed from the argument because it does no independent evidential work.

assessment.summary: A tidy observation that c011 sits badly with the argument's own theology, but as proposed it rehearses the skeptical-theism debate without engaging it and stays noncommittal on the one question that would make it a paper.

revision.research_question: Does a Molinist account of providence make the observed distribution of suffering evidentially neutral, or does it leave that distribution with an inscrutable likelihood that cannot settle a comparison with naturalism?
revision.paper_direction: A paper here would argue that the Mara case establishes a narrower point than the original claim. Molinist providence shows that the absence of a directional moral signature in history is permitted by theism, but it does not show that this absence is expected on theism. The paper would therefore replace the 'expected signature' premise (c011) with the weaker claim that theism's likelihood for the observed distribution is not fixed by the argument's own theology, given c038 and c039. It would then argue that this inscrutability does not, by itself, amount to evidential neutrality. Neutrality requires that the likelihood ratio be one, and the Molinist has supplied no basis for that. The paper's positive commitment is limited to a single claim. The comparative verdict between theism and naturalism on the historical distribution cannot be drawn from worldly randomness alone unless one supplies a prior over the counterfactuals of freedom, which the paper does not do. The paper would argue that the mp in the argument (arg1) therefore loses its second premise and that c041 must be restated as a conditional claim about what the historical evidence can and cannot adjudicate given that prior. The paper would not argue that naturalism's definite prediction is thereby defeated, and it would concede that a comparison of the two likelihoods, if one could be made, could still favor naturalism.

assessment.summary: A tidy but largely familiar point about permission versus expectation that leaves its one novel claim, that naturalism makes no definite prediction, unargued, so a competent referee would send it back as not yet a paper.

research_question: Can a Vanstone-style conception of vulnerable divine love require God to provide an intelligible, non-coercive opportunity for relationship without requiring the pursuit-based access that Schellenberg’s parental analogy attributes to perfect love?
paper_title: Some critical reflections on the hiddenness argument

challenged_premise.text: Schellenberg’s analogical argument for P1 is unsuccessful because it distorts Vanstone’s vulnerable conception of divine love.

paper_direction: A paper here would argue that the decisive issue is not whether vulnerable love permits unanswered love, but whether it requires a recognizable and non-coercive form of divine availability. It would distinguish availability from pursuit, argue that Mara-style restraint undermines any inference from perfect love to pressure or repeated intervention, and assess whether Schellenberg’s analogy can instead support a thinner requirement of intelligible access. The strongest reply to anticipate is that kenotic love still seeks the beloved’s good and makes itself available; the paper would need to show either that this requirement is satisfied despite hiddenness or that the vulnerable conception does not entail it in the relevant sense.

assessment.summary: As framed, this targets a pursuit-based reading of P1 that Schellenberg does not hold, and its own proposed refinement collapses into his openness premise, so it needs to be rebuilt around whether vulnerable love entails openness to nonresistant persons before it is a paper.

revision.research_question: Does a Vanstone-style conception of vulnerable divine love entail that God must keep relationship recognizably available to nonresistant nonbelievers, such as Tom, in the openness sense that Schellenberg's analogy requires, or does the analogy only hold for resistant refusal?
revision.paper_direction: A paper here would argue that the challenge to Schellenberg's analogy (c064) succeeds only in a narrower form than originally proposed. Schellenberg's P1 is an openness requirement restricted to nonresistant persons, and the parental analogy is offered to support that requirement, not a pursuit model. The paper therefore drops the claim that the analogy misrepresents Vanstone's conception in general. It defends a restricted thesis: the vulnerable conception, as the paper reads it, does not by itself yield the recognizable-availability requirement for nonresistant nonbelievers. The argument proceeds in three steps. First, it states Schellenberg's openness formulation exactly and separates the resistant-refusal case (the adult child) from the nonresistant case (Tom, who never asked), since only the second bears on P1. Second, it gives an independent reading of vulnerable love, in which self-giving love accepts being unanswered and does not guarantee that its offer is perceived. On this reading, non-coercive availability is satisfied by the absence of withdrawal and force, and need not include a perceivable offer to every nonresistant person. Third, it tests whether the analogy can be transferred to Tom's case without importing a control model, and it finds that the parental intuition depends on the child's recognizable access to the parent, which is exactly what is in question. The paper does not claim that hiddenness is compatible with availability. That would be a different paper about the sufficiency of evidence. Its contribution is limited to showing that the vulnerable conception does not establish the openness premise for nonresistant nonbelief, which leaves the hiddenness debate's central premise contested rather than refuted.

assessment.summary: As written, this is a narrowed restatement of a misaimed objection: unless the student can show from Vanstone that vulnerable love does not require a recognizable offer, a competent referee will treat it as begging the question against P1.
